children: 1231 ET - Treasury yields decline from multi-year highs, but elevated borrowing costs could be a new normal as a combination of drivers undermine demand for government debt. "I think a major factor is, basically, a big demand for capital from the AI buildout," Societe Generale's Jan Groen says. "And on top of that, we have a lot of demand from the federal government [and] a lot of uncertainty about the Fed, whether they actually will start hiking." Groen expects the Fed to start hiking this week and repeat every other meeting through March. Fiscal worries, however, are here to stay. "There is a real risk that fiscal dominance will be an issue for monetary policy going forward," he says. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1230 ET - Underlying price pressures in Canada remain contained, and the share of categories in the consumer-price index continue to be benign, Nomura's Ruchir Sharma says. The economist says that despite higher input costs the pass through to consumer prices has been limited. Shelter inflation picked up modestly in August but remained below 2%, and recent data suggests market rents continue to decline, and goods inflation remains soft while food inflation continues to cool. "Overall, the August report suggests inflation remains subdued and close to the Bank of Canada's target," says Sharma, who continues to expect interest rates to remain on hold through 2026. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

1218 ET - National Bank of Canada economist Mathieu Arseneau says it would be "premature" for the Bank of Canada to raise rates in October, even though headline inflation remains elevated and fears intensify over a prolonged Mideast conflict. Arseneau says core CPI remains "generally contained" near 2%, wage gains have sharply decelerated and US trade policy remains a stiff headwind. He adds the inflation data still suggests the energy shock is not, at this time, spilling over broadly into the CPI basket of goods. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1215 ET - Scotiabank's Derek Holt reckons the latest data strongly suggests the Bank of Canada is behind the curve in fighting inflation. The consumer-price index dipped 0.1% on-month in August and was steady at 3% annually. However, Holt says traditional core CPI excluding food and energy landed at 3.9% on-month seasonally adjusted, annualized, which is the hottest since April 2025. The three-moving average is 3.6% on the same basis, and the four-month average is 3.6%, he adds. Core inflation is on a tear in Canada and that continues to support an interest rate increase at the Bank of Canada's October meeting, Holt argues. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

1157 ET - The yield on Canada's two-year government bond trades at 3.41%, or the highest level in over two years — or July 31, 2024. Back in July of 2024, the Bank of Canada's policy rate was at 4.50%, on a downward trend after taming historically high inflation. The two-year yield is now 50 basis points higher from a low reached in late August, and this reflects growing concern over inflation and the need for higher interest rates. Some economists note the BOC doesn't necessarily need to raise rates given the gap between the policy rate, at 2.25%, and the 2-year yield, because the selloff in the bond market is de facto tightening monetary conditions. (paul.vieira@wsj.com)

1123 ET - August's retail sales, due Wednesday, should see a rebound from a sharp drop in July, according to an analysis from BofA. A positive reading paired with August's better-than-expected jobs report should reassure investors the economy was stronger than July's jobs report and retail sales suggested. The slide in July retail sales was due to Prime Day and related promotions shifting to June from July this year, BofA says. In August, total BAC card spending per household was up 4.5% year-over-year, according to the economists. Overall, August retail sales are expected to climb 0.8% according to WSJ consensus versus a 0.6% decline in July.(jessica.coacci@wsj.com)

1117 ET - Investors have sharply raised their expectations of Bank of England interest-rate increases over the coming months after Brent crude advanced above $109 a barrel. Markets see a 47% probability of a BOE rate rise at Thursday's policy decision, and fully price in two rate rises by year-end, LSEG data show. Traders are fully pricing in four BOE rate increases by April 2027, a notable increase from the two priced in a week ago, according to LSEG data. As a result, U.K. 2-year gilt yields have surged to 4.979%, their highest since 2023, the LSEG data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

1057 ET - New home construction is starting to slow, Zillow says. Completion of detached single-family homes fell for the third straight year in 2025, and the pace of permitting is slipping further below its pre-pandemic trend line. The concern is that a thinner pipeline could deepen an already significant housing shortage at a time when affordability is already stretched thin. Over the 12 months ending July 2026, more than 1.42 million residential building permits were issued nationwide, down 1.7% from the same period a year earlier. Compared with the pre-pandemic trajectory from 2016 through 2020, permitting is running 19.4% below where it would have been if that trend had held. Permitting has fallen year over year for 44 consecutive months. (chris.wack@wsj.com)

1052 ET - The dollar strengthens as U.S. interest rates keep rising. "The combination of heightened expectations for the Federal Reserve to lift rates late this week coupled with the high oil prices have helped lift the U.S. dollar broadly today," Bannockburn's Marc Chandler writes. The WSJ Dollar Index is up 0.5%, as the greenback strengthens 0.8% against the yen and 0.6% versus the euro. Inflation expectations are rising, as measured by the derivatives market, while Treasury yields reach multi-year highs and the 10-year benchmark surpasses 5%. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

0958 ET - Canada inflation data for August is likely to ease the likelihood of a Bank of Canada rate increase next month, says Dominique Lapointe, economist at Manulife Investment Management. Total inflation fell in August from July, and core inflation remained close to 2%. Price pressures appear to have firmed in 3Q, Lapointe says, but "the magnitude of the pickup remains contained and does not suggest meaningful second-round effects from the Iran conflict." Lapointe says he's sticking to his call for no BOC rate hike in 2026, partly because of weaker growth stemming from new U.S. tariffs and elevated trade uncertainty. (Paul.Vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

0946 ET - Yields on U.K. ten-year government bonds, or gilts, rise to their highest since 2007 while two-year gilt yields reach their highest since 2023. The moves come as rising oil prices raise inflation concerns and cause investors to ramp up expectations of the Bank of England increasing interest rates in the coming months. Brent crude price climbs 4.5% to $109.3 per barrel. Markets expect the BOE to hold rates on Thursday, but fully price four rate hikes by April 2027, LSEG data show, a notable increase from last week's pricing of two rate rises in this timeframe. Ten-year gilt yields hit a high of 5.418% while two-year gilt yields climb more than 10 basis points to 4.942%, LSEG data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0937 ET - Core inflation in Canada was largely unchanged in August from the prior month but is starting to drift upward, says Leslie Preston, economist at TD Bank. That's fueling bets of imminent rate hikes, with Preston noting the yield on 2-year Canada government bonds has jumped 40 basis points over the past month. The August CPI report does not "support this degree of tightening," Preston argues. Core CPI may be moving upward but from a low level, she says, and is likely to stay in the BOC's comfort zone. She adds growth is expected to slow due to fresh uncertainty on the US-Canada trade front. (Paul.Vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)
